sentences.text: Fossil evidence indicates that this dinosaur reached a length of approximately 8 meters.
At the Salitral Ojo del Agua site, this species was notably larger than the other sauropods found there.
The species was formally named and described in 2021 by a team led by Mauro Aranciaga Rolando.
In 2022, this species was officially designated as the type species for the new genus.
The genus name merges a Mapudungun term for a watering hole with a Latin word meaning higher.
The specific name pays tribute to Beto Arriagada, the ranch owner where the fossils were unearthed.
Bone structure analysis places the animal within the parent group known as Eutitanosauria.
However, researchers believe it does not belong to Colossosauria, Saltasaurinae, or Aeolosaurini based on its skeletal form.
Its tail vertebrae are characterized by short front-to-back lengths and tall top-to-bottom heights.
A unique trait is the lack of clear ventral grooves on the initial tail bones.
The preserved material includes a sturdy right upper arm bone, although its joint surface is missing.
Scientists propose that varied body plans among these coexisting giants allowed them to share different ecological roles.
This diversity in shape likely helped limit competition for resources within their environment.
This giant lived during the Late Cretaceous, roughly 70 million years ago, in what is now South America.
Its time range spans the Maastrichtian stage, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
It shared its habitat in the Allen Formation with other titanosaurs such as the small saltasaurine Rocasaurus.
Recent studies suggest there might be a sauropod taxon in the Allen Formation distinct from Aeolosaurus rionegrinus, Bonatitan, Menucocelsior, and Rocasaurus.
